lessons.title: It's Not You, It's the Design
lessons.key_idea: Habits fail because of poor design rather than weak willpower, so you can stop blaming yourself and start redesigning.

lessons.title: Motivation, Ability, Prompt: The Behavior Formula
lessons.key_idea: Any behavior happens only when motivation, ability, and a prompt all come together at the same moment.

lessons.title: Pick Habits You Actually Want
lessons.key_idea: Choose golden behaviors that you want to do, that make a real impact, and that you can actually do, rather than relying on fickle motivation.

lessons.title: Make It Tiny
lessons.key_idea: Shrink a new habit until it's so easy you can do it even on your worst day, like flossing just one tooth.

lessons.title: Anchor It to Your Routine
lessons.key_idea: Attach each tiny habit to something you already do with a simple recipe: after I do this, I will do that.

lessons.title: Celebrate to Wire It In
lessons.key_idea: A quick moment of celebration right after the behavior creates a feeling of success, and that feeling is what makes a habit stick.

lessons.key_idea: Tiny habits naturally grow and multiply, and the same design principles used in reverse help you dismantle unwanted habits.

plan.title: Tiny Habits
plan.author: BJ Fogg
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's core framework and main methods well, including the Fogg Behavior Model, the habit recipe format, celebration, and behavior swarming, though I'm less certain of every case study's details.
plan.one_liner: Stop blaming yourself. Change becomes easy when you design habits tiny, anchored, and celebrated.
plan.summary: BJ Fogg, a Stanford behavior scientist, argues that most attempts at change fail because of bad design, not weak character. His model says a behavior happens when motivation, ability, and a prompt come together at the same moment. Motivation rises and falls, so you shouldn't rely on it. Instead, make the new behavior so small it's almost effortless. Then attach it to something you already do every day, like flossing one tooth after brushing. Right after you do it, celebrate to create a feeling of success, because emotions are what wire habits in. Small habits then naturally grow and spread into bigger changes. The same principles, used in reverse, help you untangle unwanted habits. The result is a kind, practical, and repeatable method for lasting change.
